READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Risk taking

A We run risks. Most of the time we ignore them; sometimes we stop and decide how to deal with them. That's life. Risks arise in sports, in business, in personal relationships; they are present in the laboratory, in political calculations, everywhere. Acting individually, we often prefer to gain some benefit by accepting some danger. Acting collectively, we make similar trade-offs.

B When society must assess risks, and those risks can be clarified, at least in part, by science, technology or mathematics, the responsibility of the research community is to be clear and complete. But that is not always so easy. Furthermore, too few people pay full attention to the best evidence, much less modify their behaviors as a result. Even when the evidence of high risk is clear - about smoking, for instance - many will deny the risk, or dispute it, or accept that it exists and still go ahead. As a former cigarette smoker, I understand denial.

C Perhaps more important than the basic facts of risk are the varied perception of it. Hearing the prediction of 60% chance of rain, or recognizing the minuscule likelihood of becoming ill from a flu shot, most people understand the right responses: take your umbrella and get your flu shot. But some, fearfully but irrationally, go to the extreme and stay at home and avoid all contact with other people. Irrational decisions occasionally affect us all. When it comes to risks the best odds do not always influence people to make the correct decision.

D In her book, The Universe and the Teacup, the science writer K. C. Cole reminds us that the risks of losing something and gaining something appear to be calculated in our minds according to quite different scales. People will risk a lot to prevent a loss, she notes; some people will rush into a burning building to save a pet. But they will usually risk very little if the only perceived outcome is a possible gain; many people won't even risk pursuing an exciting job, if the current job, though unfulfilling, remains comfortable. That psychological mechanism, a desire to maintain the status quo, helps explain the high hurdles that any rational risk assessment must confront.

E Organizations face the same hurdles whenever they must cope with major shifts in policy. In his classic examination of the character of high-tech industry, Only the Paranoid Survive, Andrew S. Grove gives a perceptive account of a crisis that took place during his tenure as Chairman of the Intel Corporation. The business environment for Intel and its competitors was transformed by a flood of low-cost memory chips from Japan, and Intel made the difficult decision to abandon its chip-making business. Such a period of change in the outside world is filled with danger, Grove notes, precisely because it is so easy for executives to try to disregard it or misinterpret the mounting evidence showing the profound risks of not making change at the very core. The distinction Cole cites is instructive here: one reason management and staff may not act is that they tend to focus on the potential gains of risking change (which they characterize as small), rather than on the catastrophic losses that risking change could prevent. The period becomes critical for a company, according to Grove, and deadly when unattended to.

F Likewise, at the national level, and even the global one, institutions tend to be more willing to take a risk if it means avoiding a loss, than they are if it might confer a gain. Almost everyone, for instance, sees the signs of ecological decay. Reid J. Lifest's article, 'Full Accounting', describes newly developed techniques for clarifying which critical decision would have the highest pay-offs for the environment. Once these 'leverage points' as he calls them, are located, many environmental organizations will be willing to risk the resources needed to prevent further deterioration.

G More complicated are decisions by nations to invest broadly in educational research. Some governmental leaders are oblivious to the risks posed by social underinvestment, because the urgent needs of the present take precedence over actions that would give rise to even more substantial gains in the future. Their attitude is that today's risks must be manageable, and that tomorrow's gains are at the very least difficult to measure. Better consideration and decision making for what lies ahead is essential.

H Nevertheless, I confess to being an optimist. My glass is generally half full - though that may not help me handle risk. Whether one's temperament is optimistic or pessimistic, everyone in our scientific and engineering community has a social responsibility: measure with care and portray with honesty the level of risk involved in any action or decision.

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Questions 27–30

Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–G, below.

Write the correct letter, A–G, in boxes 27–30 on your answer sheet.

List of endings:
  • A planning for the future.
  • B predicting their errors.
  • C continuing in the present situation.
  • D recent findings on the most effective solutions to problems.
  • E achieving a gain.
  • F changes occurring externally.
  • G a high level of agreement.

27. K. C. Cole points out that avoiding a loss seems more important to people than ______.

28. According to Andrew S. Grove, it can be very dangerous for companies to ignore ______.

29. Reid J. Lifset argues that environmental agencies can benefit from ______.

30. The writer suggests that government leaders need to focus more on ______.

Questions 31–39

The reading passage has eight paragraphs, A–H.

Which paragraph contains the following information?

Write the correct letter, A–H, in boxes 31–39 on your answer sheet.

NB You may use any letter more than once.

31. the areas of study that help us understand risk
32. reference to key actions that might benefit the world
33. examples of statistical predictions that the majority of the public react to in the same way
34. the variety of contexts in which risk occurs
35. mention of a habit that has been proved to be very risky
36. reference to market forces motivating change
37. the writer's current attitude towards risk
38. a reason why some individuals avoid making a career change
39. how some people over-react to information about risk

Question 40

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

40. At the end of the passage the writer concludes that

passageNotes.label: Paragraph A
passageNotes.text: 我们承担风险。大多数时候我们忽视它们；有时我们会停下来决定如何应对它们。这就是生活。风险出现在体育运动中、商业中、人际关系中；它们存在于实验室中、政治考量中，无处不在。作为个体行动时，我们往往愿意通过接受某些危险来获得某些利益。集体行动时，我们也会做出类似的权衡。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph B
passageNotes.text: 当社会必须评估风险，而这些风险至少可以部分地通过科学、技术或数学来澄清时，研究界的责任是清晰和完整地表达。但这并不总是那么容易。此外，很少有人充分关注最佳证据，更不用说因此改变自己的行为了。即使高风险的证据很清楚——例如关于吸烟的证据——许多人也会否认风险，或质疑它，或接受它存在但仍然继续。作为一个曾经的吸烟者，我理解这种否认心理。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph C
passageNotes.text: 也许比风险的基本事实更重要的是对风险的各种不同认知。听到60%降雨概率的预测，或者认识到因流感疫苗接种而生病的微小可能性，大多数人理解正确的应对方式：带上雨伞并接种流感疫苗。但有些人，出于恐惧但非理性地，走向极端，待在家里，避免与其他人接触。非理性的决定偶尔会影响我们所有人。当涉及到风险时，最好的赔率并不总是能影响人们做出正确的决定。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph D
passageNotes.text: 科学作家K. C. Cole在她的书《宇宙与茶杯》中提醒我们，失去某物和获得某物的风险似乎在我们的头脑中按照完全不同的尺度来计算。她指出，人们会冒着很大风险来防止损失；有些人会冲进着火的建筑去救宠物。但如果唯一可感知的结果是可能的收益，他们通常只会冒很小的风险；许多人甚至不会冒险去追求一份令人兴奋的工作，如果当前的工作虽然不尽如人意但仍然舒适的话。这种心理机制，即维持现状的欲望，有助于解释任何理性风险评估都必须面对的巨大障碍。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph E
passageNotes.text: 每当组织必须应对政策的重大转变时，它们也面临着同样的障碍。安德鲁·S·格鲁夫（Andrew S. Grove）在其对高科技行业特征的经典研究《只有偏执狂才能生存》中，对他在担任英特尔公司董事长期间发生的一场危机进行了深刻的描述。英特尔及其竞争对手的商业环境被来自日本的廉价存储芯片洪流所改变，英特尔做出了放弃芯片制造业务的艰难决定。格鲁夫指出，外部世界发生如此变化的时期充满了危险，恰恰是因为高管们很容易试图忽视它或误解越来越多的证据，这些证据显示了不在核心层面做出改变的深刻风险。Cole引用的区分在这里很有启发性：管理层和员工可能不采取行动的一个原因是，他们倾向于关注冒险改变的潜在收益（他们将其描述为很小），而不是关注冒险改变可能避免的灾难性损失。格鲁夫认为，这个时期对公司来说变得至关重要，如果被忽视则是致命的。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph F
passageNotes.text: 同样，在国家层面，甚至全球层面，机构往往更愿意承担风险，如果这意味着避免损失，而不是可能带来收益。例如，几乎每个人都看到了生态衰退的迹象。Reid J. Lifset的文章《全面核算》描述了新开发的技术，用于阐明哪些关键决策将对环境产生最高的回报。一旦这些他所谓的“杠杆点”被找到，许多环境组织将愿意冒所需的资源风险来防止进一步的恶化。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph G
passageNotes.text: 更复杂的是各国广泛投资教育研究的决策。一些政府领导人无视社会投资不足所带来的风险，因为当前的紧迫需求优先于那些将在未来产生更实质性收益的行动。他们的态度是，今天的风险必须是可控的，而明天的收益至少是难以衡量的。更好地考虑和决策未来是至关重要的。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph H
passageNotes.text: 然而，我承认自己是一个乐观主义者。我的杯子通常是半满的——尽管这可能无助于我处理风险。无论一个人的性情是乐观还是悲观，我们科学和工程界的每个人都有社会责任：仔细衡量并诚实地描绘任何行动或决策所涉及的风险水平。
